steps.why: The process turns on one physical fact: the hydrogen carbonate formed must be insoluble enough to come out of solution, because settling out as a solid is how it is separated from everything else in the solution.
common_mistakes: Writing that sodium hydrogen carbonate is insoluble. It is sparingly soluble, which is just low enough for it to precipitate.
Describing the whole Solvay process. The step this question turns on is the precipitation; the rest of the process is not needed to answer it.
steps.memory_tip: The process works only because the hydrogen carbonate comes out as a solid.
steps.margin_note: Show the precipitation step first, then give the reason for potassium.

steps.label: Why the process stops for potassium
lines: too soluble in water to precipitate.
It stays in solution, so the separation
step never happens and the process

Potassium carbonate is therefore made by
steps.why: Solubility is the single difference between the two metals here. KHCO₃ dissolves far more readily than NaHCO₃, so nothing settles out and the Solvay route has no way to collect its product.
common_mistakes: Writing that potassium does not react with ammonium hydrogen carbonate. It does react; the product simply stays dissolved.
Naming the larger size of the potassium ion without saying what it leads to — the high solubility of KHCO₃.
steps.memory_tip: KHCO₃ stays dissolved, so there is nothing to filter off.
steps.margin_note: The one word that answers this question is soluble.

insider_note: This rests on one idea — KHCO₃ is too soluble to precipitate — but a complete answer first shows the step in the process that needs a precipitate.
